name: Alternative Technologies
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Beyond the Chain: Tools That Solve the Same Problems
lesson.summary: Many problems people reach for blockchain to solve already have simpler, cheaper solutions in distributed databases, traditional PKI, and append-only logs, and recognizing when these alternatives fit is a core skeptic skill.
lesson.body:
Recall from Blockchain Definition that a blockchain is a specific engineering solution to a specific problem: how mutually distrusting parties can agree on a shared, tamper-evident record without a trusted intermediary. That is a narrow, expensive problem to solve, and most data problems are not actually that problem.

Recall Centralized Database: a single organization owning the data, fast transactions, no consensus overhead to pay for. If only one party writes to a system, or if one party is already trusted by everyone else to arbitrate disputes, a centralized database beats a blockchain on almost every practical metric: cost, speed, query flexibility, and the simple ability to fix a mistake.

Distributed databases are not the same thing as blockchains, even though the two get confused. Systems like Apache Cassandra, CockroachDB, or Google Spanner replicate data across many machines for availability and disaster recovery, but those machines are all controlled by one organization. They use consensus protocols such as Raft or Paxos, mathematically related to blockchain consensus, but without proof of work, mining rewards, or public verifiability, because there is no need to defend against a malicious minority of anonymous strangers.

Traditional PKI vs DLT already introduced another working alternative: certificate authorities provide a trust model for identity and digital signatures used across the entire web through TLS certificates, with no blockchain involved anywhere. PKI answers the question of how you know a given public key belongs to a given entity, through a hierarchy of trusted certificate authorities. It has real weaknesses, most notably a single compromised or coerced authority, but for many use cases those weaknesses are acceptable given how much cheaper and faster PKI is than a blockchain-based alternative.

A few other alternatives are worth knowing. Append-only logs and Merkle trees can provide tamper evidence without full blockchain consensus, the way Certificate Transparency logs let browsers catch rogue TLS certificates. Content-addressed storage, the same idea git uses to identify files by their hash, provides integrity checking without a chain at all. And when participants already trust each other's identities through ordinary PKI, they can simply exchange digitally signed documents among a known, fixed set of parties, with no need for open membership or a shared ledger.

The habit this chapter is meant to build is simple: before reaching for a blockchain, ask what specific problem you are solving and whether trust already exists through a workable alternative. The next chapter turns that question into an explicit decision framework, and later chapters on hybrid architecture will show how blockchains and these very alternatives often end up working side by side rather than as competitors.
